summary.text: A 75-year-old man with hypertension, who had undergone an open appendectomy for perforated acute appendicitis six months prior, presented to his primary care physician with a five-month history of persistent, dull, intermittent right upper quadrant pain. He denied fever, chills and jaundice. He had mild RUQ tenderness without peritoneal signs, moderately elevated C-reactive protein and sedimentation rate, a mildly elevated white blood cell count of 11×10^(9)/L, and normal liver enzymes.

Ultrasound showed a 2.8 cm cystic-appearing lesion at the inferior right hepatic lobe, initially interpreted as a possible simple liver cyst. A follow-up MRI one month later showed a rim-enhancing fluid collection of about 3 cm posterior to the right hepatic lobe, consistent with a localized abscess. Review of prior imaging showed two calcified appendicoliths on the CT done at appendicitis diagnosis and a new subhepatic radiodensity of about 1 cm on a post-operative CT, indicating that one appendicolith had migrated.

Hepatic abscess secondary to a retained appendicolith was diagnosed and he was admitted. Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics were started, interventional radiology was consulted, and ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage aspirated about 30 mL of purulent fluid with a pigtail catheter left in place. Fluid culture grew Escherichia coli and antibiotics were tailored to sensitivities. The appendicolith was not retrieved, and conservative management was decided.

Pain and inflammatory markers improved markedly over the next week with no drainage complications. The drain was removed after one week, follow-up ultrasound showed collapse of the abscess cavity, and CT one month after drainage showed complete resolution with the appendicolith still visible. At three months he was asymptomatic on oral antibiotics; he declined further surgery, and long-term follow-up details are not available.
